name: AI in Regulatory Submissions
blurb: How much AI appears in drug submissions, and AI written submission documents.
title: AI in Regulatory Submissions
answer: AI has become routine in drug submissions. FDA staff counted one submission with AI components a year in 2016 and 2017 and 132 in 2021, and the agency later cited more than 500 from 2016 to 2023. Sponsors also use generative AI to draft submission documents such as nonclinical summaries, with reported large time savings, but the sponsor remains accountable for every statement.

reading.body:
AI has moved from rare to routine in drug submissions, with FDA staff counting 132 submissions containing AI components in 2021 against one a year in 2016 and 2017.

The adoption curve is steep and one-directional. A single submission in 2016 and 2017 became 132 in 2021, and the agency later cited more than 500 across 2016 to 2023. That is not a pilot pattern. It is the shape of a tool that sponsors adopted once it worked, and it means reviewers now encounter AI-derived content as a normal case rather than an exception.

The second shift is in who writes the document. Generative AI drafting cut the time to produce nonclinical IND summaries from roughly 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours per batch, with no critical regulatory errors found under the study's criteria. The accountability does not move with the time saved. The sponsor remains answerable for every statement, which is why the practical requirement is a trail linking each drafted claim back to its source and disclosure of where AI produced regulatory data.

What this data does not cover is the quality of those 500-plus submissions, how the FDA assessed them, or whether the time savings hold outside the nonclinical summaries studied. It also gives no count of submissions where AI use went undisclosed. The numbers establish adoption and drafting speed, not review outcomes.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.

Models that create new content, text, images, video, audio, code, from patterns learned in training data. The 2022 shift from AI that classifies to AI that produces is what put this glossary on your reading list.

The subset of AI focused on systems that learn from data and improve with experience rather than following explicitly programmed rules. Nearly everything called AI in production is machine learning underneath.

explainer:
AI shows up in submissions in two different ways. The first is AI as part of the evidence: models used to identify patients, measure endpoints, analyse images, predict pharmacokinetics or support manufacturing controls. These uses have grown steadily, and they are what the FDA's credibility framework addresses. Sponsors should describe such models, their context of use and their validation in the submission.

The second is AI as a writing tool: generative models drafting nonclinical and clinical summaries, investigator brochures and other templated documents. Studies report large reductions in drafting time for specific document types, but they also report errors that reviewers must catch, and the time saved in drafting partly moves to verification. Agencies do not treat AI drafted text differently, so the sponsor's normal quality process applies in full. The sensible approach is to use AI where documents are highly structured and source data are clean, and to verify every figure and claim against its source.

developments.text: An FDA analysis in Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics found submissions with AI or machine learning components rose to 132 in 2021.

A study posted on arXiv reported AI drafting cut the time to write nonclinical IND summaries from about 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours per batch, with no critical regulatory errors found under its criteria.
